title: Chicken fajitas
skill: Julienne: peppers and onions in thin strips

notes.text: For more than 6, sear the chicken in two batches so the pan stays hot, and cook the vegetables in two batches too.

move.title: Strips, then sizzle
move.body: Julienne means cutting food into thin, even strips. Today you'll cut peppers and onions that way, sear seasoned chicken in a very hot pan, and pile it all into warm tortillas.

why.title: Skin side down
why.body: The shiny skin of a pepper is slippery, and a knife can skate right off it. Lay the pepper skin side down and cut into the soft inside instead. The knife grips, and the strips come out even.

why.title: Same size, same time
why.body: Thin strips cook faster than thick ones. When every strip is about the same size, they all turn soft and brown at the same moment, with no burnt bits and no raw ones.

why.title: Leave it alone to brown
why.body: Browning happens where the chicken touches the hot pan. If you keep moving it, it never gets the chance. At first the chicken sticks, but once a brown crust forms, it lets go by itself. That's how you know it's ready to flip.

why.title: Why the chicken rests
why.body: Right out of the pan, the juice inside hot meat is moving around fast. Cut it now and the juice runs out onto the board. Five minutes of rest lets it settle, so it stays in the chicken.

wrong.sign: The chicken is stuck to the pan
wrong.fix: Wait another minute. When the bottom is browned, it lets go by itself.

wrong.sign: The vegetables are pale and watery
wrong.fix: The pan is too crowded or not hot enough. Turn up the heat, spread them out, and give them time before you stir.

wrong.sign: Some strips burned while others are still crunchy
wrong.fix: The strips were different sizes. Pull out the done ones and let the rest catch up. Next time, aim for strips the same width.

quiz.q: Which way up does the pepper go when you cut it?
quiz.explain: The knife can slip on the shiny skin. Cutting into the soft inside is safer and makes neater strips.

quiz.q: How do you know the chicken is ready to flip?
choices: It lets go of the pan by itself
It has been in for one minute
quiz.explain: Once a brown crust forms, the chicken releases from the pan.

substitutions.note: Warm corn tortillas two at a time, and use two per fajita if they tear.

steps.text: Cut the top and bottom off each pepper. Stand it up, cut down one side, and open it out into one long, flat strip. Cut away the seeds and the white ribs.
steps.tip: Hold the food with your hand shaped like a claw: fingertips tucked under, knuckles in front.

steps.text: Lay each pepper skin side down and julienne it: cut it into thin strips, about as wide as a pencil.
steps.look: A pile of strips that are all about the same width.

steps.text: Cut the onion in half from top to bottom, through the root. Peel off the papery skin. Lay each half flat side down and cut thin strips from end to end, the same width as the peppers.
steps.tip: The flat side keeps the onion half from rolling.

steps.text: In the small bowl, stir together the chili powder, cumin, garlic powder, smoked paprika, {qty:salt} salt, the lime juice, and {qty:olive-oil} olive oil.
Lay the chicken on the plate. Spread the spice paste over both sides with your hands, and leave it there while the pan heats.
Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw chicken or its package touched.
Heat 1 tablespoon of the vegetable oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
Use the tongs to lay the chicken in the pan, smooth side down, with space between the pieces. Put the tongs in the sink, and don't use them again for cooked food.
steps.tip: Lay each piece down away from you, so any spatter goes the other way.

steps.text: Wash your hands, and put the raw-chicken plate in the sink. From here on, use the clean spatula.
Leave the chicken alone. Don't poke it or move it while the bottom browns.
steps.look: A deep brown crust, and it lets go of the pan when you nudge it.

steps.text: Flip each piece with the spatula and sear the other side.
Slide the thermometer into the thickest piece. It needs to read at least 165°F. If it doesn't, cook 2 more minutes and check again.
Move the chicken to the clean cutting board with the spatula and let it rest.
Add the rest of the vegetable oil to the same pan, then the peppers and onion. Spread them out and let them sizzle, stirring every minute or so, until soft and browned at the edges.
steps.look: Soft, bendy strips with brown spots.
steps.tip: Scrape up the brown bits the chicken left behind. They're full of flavor.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Stack the tortillas, wrap them in a damp paper towel, and microwave until warm and soft.
steps.tip: The steam inside is hot. Open the paper towel slowly.

steps.text: Slice the rested chicken into thin strips.
Put the chicken back in the pan with the vegetables and stir. Fill the warm tortillas and top them with sour cream, salsa, avocado, or cilantro if you're using them.
steps.tip: The handle stays hot for a long time. Leave an oven mitt on it so nobody grabs it bare-handed.

notes.text: For more than 6, sear the steak in two batches so the pan stays hot, and cook the vegetables in two batches too.

season.text: Lay the steak on the plate and pat it dry with paper towels. Spread the spice paste over both sides with your hands, and leave it there while the pan heats.

wash-season.text: Throw the paper towels away. Wash your hands with soap, and wipe anything the raw steak or its package touched.

add-chicken.text: Use the tongs to lay the steak in the pan, laying it down away from you. Put the tongs in the sink, and don't use them again for cooked food.
add-chicken.tip: If the steak is too long for the pan, cut it in half first, before it gets its spice paste.

wash-pan.text: Wash your hands, and put the raw-steak plate in the sink. From here on, use the clean spatula.

sear.text: Leave the steak alone. Don't poke it or move it while the bottom browns.
sear.look: A deep brown crust, and it lets go of the pan when you nudge it.

flip.text: Flip the steak with the spatula and sear the other side.

check-chicken.text: Slide the thermometer into the side of the steak, into the thickest part. It needs to read at least 145°F. If it doesn't, cook 1 more minute on each side and check again.

rest.text: Move the steak to the clean cutting board with the spatula and let it rest.

vegetables.text: Add the rest of the vegetable oil to the same pan, then the peppers and onion. Spread them out and let them sizzle, stirring every minute or so, until soft and browned at the edges.
vegetables.look: Soft, bendy strips with brown spots.
vegetables.tip: Scrape up the brown bits the steak left behind. They're full of flavor.

slice.text: Look for the thin lines running along the steak. Turn it so they run left to right, and slice it into thin strips, across the lines.
slice.look: Each strip shows short little lines across its cut face, not long strings.

serve.text: Put the steak back in the pan with the vegetables and stir. Fill the warm tortillas and top them with sour cream, salsa, avocado, or cilantro if you're using them.
serve.tip: The handle stays hot for a long time. Leave an oven mitt on it so nobody grabs it bare-handed.

move.title: Strips, then sizzle
move.body: Julienne means cutting food into thin, even strips. Today you'll cut peppers and onions that way, sear a seasoned flank steak in a very hot pan, slice it thin, and pile it all into warm tortillas.

wrong.sign: The steak is stuck to the pan
wrong.fix: Wait another minute. When the bottom is browned, it lets go by itself.

wrong.sign: The vegetables are pale and watery
wrong.fix: The pan is too crowded or not hot enough. Turn up the heat, spread them out, and give them time before you stir.

wrong.sign: Some strips burned while others are still crunchy
wrong.fix: The strips were different sizes. Pull out the done ones and let the rest catch up. Next time, aim for strips the same width.
They were cut along the grain. Turn the steak a quarter turn and slice the rest the other way, thinner.

quiz.q: Which way up does the pepper go when you cut it?
quiz.explain: The knife can slip on the shiny skin. Cutting into the soft inside is safer and makes neater strips.

quiz.q: Which way do you slice the cooked steak?
choices: Along the lines in the meat
Across the lines in the meat
quiz.explain: Slicing across the grain makes short fibers, so every strip is tender.

leave-it.title: Leave it alone to brown
leave-it.body: Browning happens where the steak touches the hot pan. If you keep moving it, it never gets the chance. At first it sticks, but once a brown crust forms, it lets go by itself. That's how you know it's ready to flip.

rest.title: Why the steak rests
rest.body: Right out of the pan, the juice inside hot meat is moving around fast. Cut it now and the juice runs out onto the board. Five minutes of rest lets it settle, so it stays in the steak.

add.title: Across the grain
add.body: Flank steak is made of long fibers, all running the same way, and you can see them as lines. Slice across those lines and every strip has short fibers that are easy to chew. Slice along them and the strips are stringy.

notes.text: For more than 6, cook the vegetables in two batches so they brown instead of steaming.

heat.text: Heat the vegetable oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.

vegetables.text: Add the peppers and onion. Spread them out and let them sizzle, stirring every minute or so, until soft and browned at the edges.
vegetables.look: Soft, bendy strips with brown spots.
vegetables.tip: Give them time before you stir. Brown spots come from sitting still on the hot pan.

serve.text: Fill the warm tortillas with the beans and vegetables, and top them with sour cream, salsa, avocado, or cilantro if you're using them.
serve.tip: The handle stays hot for a long time. Leave an oven mitt on it so nobody grabs it bare-handed.

add.text: Open the cans of beans and pour them into the colander in the sink. Rinse them with cold water until the bubbles are gone, and let them drain.
add.tip: Keep your fingers away from the cut edge of the lid. It's as sharp as a knife.

add.text: Add the beans and the spice paste to the pan. Stir gently with the wooden spoon until the beans are hot and coated.
add.look: The beans are shiny with spices and steaming hot.

move.title: Strips, then sizzle
move.body: Julienne means cutting food into thin, even strips. Today you'll cut peppers and onions that way, sizzle them in a hot pan, stir in spiced black beans, and pile it all into warm tortillas.

wrong.sign: The beans are mushy and falling apart
wrong.fix: They only need warming. Stir gently, and take the pan off the heat as soon as they're hot.

wrong.sign: The vegetables are pale and watery
wrong.fix: The pan is too crowded or not hot enough. Turn up the heat, spread them out, and give them time before you stir.

wrong.sign: Some strips burned while others are still crunchy
wrong.fix: The strips were different sizes. Pull out the done ones and let the rest catch up. Next time, aim for strips the same width.

quiz.q: Which way up does the pepper go when you cut it?
quiz.explain: The knife can slip on the shiny skin. Cutting into the soft inside is safer and makes neater strips.

quiz.q: Why do you rinse canned beans?
choices: To wash off the thick, salty liquid
quiz.explain: The canning liquid is starchy and salty. Rinsing it off lets your spices flavor the beans.

add.title: Why rinse the beans
add.body: The liquid in a can of beans is thick, starchy, and salty. Rinsing it off in the colander lets the spices, not the can, flavor the beans, and keeps the filling from turning gluey.

spice-paste.text: In the small bowl, stir together the chili powder, cumin, garlic powder, smoked paprika, cayenne, {qty:salt} salt, the lime juice, and {qty:olive-oil} olive oil.

vegetables.text: Add the rest of the vegetable oil to the same pan, then the peppers, jalapeños, and onion. Spread them out and let them sizzle, stirring every minute or so, until soft and browned at the edges.
vegetables.look: Soft, bendy strips with brown spots.
vegetables.tip: Scrape up the brown bits the chicken left behind. They're full of flavor.

add.text: Cut the jalapeños in half from top to bottom. Scrape out the seeds and white ribs with the spoon, then julienne each half into thin strips like the peppers.
add.tip: Wash your hands with soap right after cutting the jalapeño. Its juice stings if it gets in your eyes.

wrong.sign: The chicken is stuck to the pan
wrong.fix: Wait another minute. When the bottom is browned, it lets go by itself.

wrong.sign: The vegetables are pale and watery
wrong.fix: The pan is too crowded or not hot enough. Turn up the heat, spread them out, and give them time before you stir.

wrong.sign: Some strips burned while others are still crunchy
wrong.fix: The strips were different sizes. Pull out the done ones and let the rest catch up. Next time, aim for strips the same width.
Pile on sour cream and avocado; they cool it down. Next time, scrape out all of the jalapeño ribs and seeds and leave out the cayenne.

add.title: Where the heat is
add.body: Most of a jalapeño's heat is in its white ribs and seeds. Scrape them out and it's warm; leave some in and it's hot. The juice stays on your fingers, so wash your hands right after cutting it, before you touch your eyes or face.
